# Implement block: Morph Bubble Column (Jetpack Compose)

You are adding the "Morph Bubble Column" block from Native Cook to the user's Android app. The block already exists as working Kotlin code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A field-survey app on a white screen with a faint dot grid, edge to edge: the date and a pixel clock reading 9:PM at the top left, a black pill at the top right with an avatar and a bolt button, a dark notch in the right edge holding three tool icons and a white bar at the bottom with a zoom slider. Down the middle runs a column of round photo bubbles, one per survey site, each with its number and name beside it. The selected site is a big rounded square with its coordinates and a hairline leading to it; dragging along the column moves the selection, and the bubbles morph between circle and rounded square as it passes. Tapping the selected site grows its bubble into the whole screen, where a monospace heading types itself behind a block cursor, a target ring locks onto the photo, a big dot-matrix reading counts up and the slider zooms into the photo; dragging down puts it back in the column.

**Motion.** The selection is one number, 0 (top site) to 4, and every bubble is as selected as that number is close to it: its width and height grow from 1 to 1.5 × 1.42 units (one unit 21% of the screen width, scaled 0.92–1.08 by the slider) linearly, while its corners (as a share of half its shorter side, 1 → 0.4) and their superellipse exponent (2, a circle's arc → 3.6, a squircle's shoulder) follow a smoothstep of it, so a half-selected bubble still reads round. The column is laid out every frame from those sizes, 14 pt between bubbles and centred between the clock and the bar, each unselected bubble set off its axis by up to 0.08 units like a hand-set column. Dragging anywhere on the column moves the selection with the finger (one site per 92 pt, rubber-banding past either end), with a selection haptic as it passes each site; on release the finger's speed carries it 0.16 s further and it settles on the nearest site on a spring (stiffness 210, damping ratio 0.82) that starts with the finger's speed. A tap on a bubble selects it (selection haptic) on a calm, critically damped spring (stiffness 70, about 0.8 s); a tap on the selected bubble opens it. The site labels sit left of their bubbles, centred on them: the selected one in ink with its coordinates and a hairline drawn out to the bubble, the others at 42%. On first appearance the bubbles bloom from a dot, top to bottom 0.11 s apart, on an underdamped spring (9 rad/s, damping ratio 0.8). Opening is a spring (stiffness 95, damping 17.5) from 0 to 1: the bubble's box, corners and squircle shoulder interpolate to the full-screen rectangle (the notch bites into it as it arrives) while the other bubbles shrink by 8% and fade and the labels fade out; a light haptic marks the open. The photo is the same portrait crop in the bubble and full screen, so a sharp copy fades in over the thumbnail without a shift; every photo fades in over 0.35 s as it arrives. Once open, the heading types one character per 60 ms after 0.7 s with a blinking block cursor (1.6 Hz once done), a target ring grows in from 1.0 s (ease-out) with its ticks turning at 14°/s, pinned to the photo as it zooms, and the reading counts from 0 over 1.6 s (ease-out) from 1.6 s in 5 × 7 dot-matrix figures, 8 pt to a pixel. The slider sets the zoom (10–90 x): it zooms the open photo by up to 20% and the column by 0.92–1.08, ticks a selection haptic every eighth of its track, and glides on a spring (stiffness 26, damping 10.2) when set by a tap or the loop. Dragging the open photo down follows the finger (60% of the screen height closes it fully, rubber-banding by 0.22 past open); releasing faster than 650 pt/s down or below 80% open closes it with the finger's speed handed to the spring and a soft haptic, otherwise it springs back open. autoPlay (LOOP = 18 s) rests on the top site, steps the selection down at 1.2 and 2.7 s, opens the third site at 4.3 s (it types, locks on and counts), glides the slider to 74 x at 8.6 s and back to 50 x at 10.8 s, closes it at 12.4 s and steps the selection back up at 14.2 and 15.6 s, so the loop ends where it began. A touch pauses the loop for 4 s (8 s after opening a photo); the loop then closes any open photo and selects the top site again. With Reduce Motion the selection jumps, the bubbles appear without blooming, a photo fades in over 0.25 s at full screen instead of growing, and the heading and reading appear complete.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [MorphBubbleColumnDemo.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/pickers/morphbubblecolumn/MorphBubbleColumnDemo.kt)

### Files of the block

- [MorphBubbleColumn.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/pickers/morphbubblecolumn/MorphBubbleColumn.kt)
- [MorphBubbleColumnEngine.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/pickers/morphbubblecolumn/MorphBubbleColumnEngine.kt)
- [MorphBubbleColumnGlyphs.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/pickers/morphbubblecolumn/MorphBubbleColumnGlyphs.kt)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/shared/ComponentSupport.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/shared/ComponentSupport.kt)

The versions the block was built with are in [kotlin/gradle/libs.versions.toml](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/gradle/libs.versions.toml).

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced Android engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference on an emulator or a device. A Compose preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build, install and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and easing. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an Android app built with Gradle. If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app module, its namespace, `minSdk`, `compileSdk`, and the versions of Kotlin, the Android Gradle Plugin and Compose (a BOM or single versions).
- Whether Compose is switched on in that module, and whether screens are Compose, Views or both.
- Navigation: Navigation Compose, fragments, activities, or a single screen. Find how a screen is added today.
- How dependencies are declared: a version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`) or directly in `build.gradle`.
- Conventions: package layout, naming, theme, where resources live and how they are named.

### 3. Read the block

- Open the demo, then each file in the block's package. The list above names every file of the block, and the resources it uses from outside its package.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's parameters and their defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- Compare the block's libraries and the versions it was built with to the host's. Add what is missing the way this project declares dependencies. Do not upgrade the host's Kotlin, Gradle plugin or Compose versions without asking; if an API differs on the host's version, adapt the block's code.
- Check `minSdk`. If the block uses an API newer than the host's minimum, keep the fallback the source has, or tell the user what would be lost.
- If Compose is not switched on in the module, say what turning it on involves before you do it. In a View-based screen, show the block through a `ComposeView`.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block imports next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.

### 5. Bring it in

- Copy the block's files into a package of this app, and rewrite the `package` lines and the imports, including the import of the app's own `R` class.
- Copy its resources and asset files. Keep their names unless one collides with a resource of the app; then rename it everywhere it is used.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility descriptions as they are in the source. If the block needs a permission, add it to the manifest and say so.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen or destination named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build with the project's own task, for example `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug`, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Install and run it, and use the block: every state, every gesture, and once with animations switched off in the system settings.
- If the build or the emulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, dependencies and permissions added, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
